changes.before: Mrs. John Dashwood thoroughly disapproved of her husband's plans for his sisters. Taking three thousand pounds from their dear little boy's fortune would impoverish him to a dreadful extent. She begged her husband to reconsider. How could he justify to himself robbing his child—his only child, too—of such an enormous sum? And what possible claim on his generosity could the Miss Dashwoods possibly have on so much generosity? They were only his half-sisters, which, in her opinion, counted as no relationship whatsoever. Everyone knew that affection was never expected between a man's children by different marriages. Why should he ruin himself and their poor little Harry by giving all his money away to his half-sisters?

changes.before: “Did I not explain, Sir John, when you first mentioned it, that it could not be done? They were the last to dine with us.”
changes.after: “Did I not explain, Sir John, when you first mentioned it, that it could not be done? The last time we dined together, we were the hosts.”

changes.before: “Nearly three years passed after that unhappy time before I returned to England. Naturally, my first concern when I _did_ arrive was to find her. But the search was as unsuccessful as it was distressing. I could trace her no further than the first man who had seduced her. There was every reason to fear that she had left him only to sink further into a life of wrongdoing. The allowance legally assigned to her was neither proportionate to her fortune nor sufficient to keep her comfortably. My brother told me that some months earlier she had transferred the right to receive it to someone else. He supposed—and could suppose it quite calmly—that extravagance and the hardship it caused had forced her to sell it for immediate relief. At last, after six months in England, I _did_ find her. Affection for a former servant who had since fallen on hard times took me to visit him in a debtors' holding house. There, in the same building and under the same confinement, was my unfortunate sister-in-law. So changed, so faded, worn down by every kind of acute suffering! I could hardly believe that the sickly, sorrowful figure before me was all that remained of the lovely, healthy, blooming girl I had once adored. What I felt on seeing her—but I have no right to hurt you by trying to describe it. I have already caused you too much pain. That she appeared to be in the final stage of consumption was—yes, in those circumstances—my greatest comfort. Life could offer her nothing except time to prepare better for death, and she was given that time. I arranged comfortable lodgings and proper care for her. I visited her every day of the short life that remained, and I was with her when she died.”

changes.before: “I hope your sister would not be offended,” he said, “by the resemblance I have imagined between her and my poor, disgraced relation. Their fates and circumstances cannot be the same. If the natural sweetness of the one had been protected by a stronger mind or a happier marriage, she might have become everything you will live to see the other become. But where is all this leading? I seem to have distressed you for nothing. Ah, Miss Dashwood, a subject like this, untouched for fourteen years—it is dangerous to approach it at all! I _will_ be more composed, more concise. She entrusted her only child to me, a little girl of about three, born from her first affair. She loved the child and had always kept her with her. It was a precious trust to me. Gladly would I have fulfilled it in the fullest sense, overseeing her education myself, if our circumstances had allowed. But I had neither family nor home, and so my little Eliza was sent to school. I visited her whenever I could. After my brother's death, about five years ago, when I inherited the family property, she visited me at Delaford. I described her as a distant relation, though I know very well that people have generally suspected a much closer connection. Three years ago, when she had just turned fourteen, I took her from school and placed her with a very respectable woman in Dorsetshire who looked after four or five other girls of about the same age. For two years I had every reason to be satisfied with the arrangement. But last February, almost a year ago, she suddenly disappeared. At her earnest request, I had allowed her—unwisely, as it turned out—to go to Bath with a young friend whose father was there for his health. I knew him as a very good sort of man, and thought well of his daughter: better than she deserved. With stubborn, ill-judged secrecy she would tell me nothing and give me no clue, though she certainly knew everything. Her father was well-meaning but not observant, and I believe he truly had no information to give. He had mostly been confined to the house while the girls wandered about the town, making whatever acquaintances they pleased. He tried to convince me, as completely as he had convinced himself, that his daughter had nothing to do with the affair. In short, I could learn only that Eliza was gone. Everything else remained a matter of conjecture for eight long months. You may imagine what I thought, what I feared, and what I suffered.”

changes.before: “The first news of her,” he continued, “came in a letter she wrote herself, last October. It was forwarded from Delaford, and reached me on the very morning of our planned outing to Whitwell. That was why I left Barton so suddenly. I am sure my departure seemed strange to everyone, and I believe it offended some. When Mr. Willoughby's looks reproached me for the discourtesy of breaking up the party, I suppose he little imagined that I was being called away to help someone he had made destitute and miserable. But if he _had_ known, what difference would it have made? Would he have been less cheerful, or taken less pleasure in your sister's smiles? No. He had already done what no man capable of feeling for another could do. He had seduced a young, innocent girl, then abandoned her in the deepest distress, without a respectable home, without help or friends, and without even knowing his address. He left her with a promise to return. He neither returned, nor wrote, nor sent assistance.”

changes.before: This event, so important to Mrs. Jennings's happiness, temporarily changed the way she spent her time and, to the same extent, the arrangements of her young guests. Wanting to be with Charlotte as much as possible, she left every morning as soon as she was dressed and returned only late in the evening. At the Middletons' special request, the Miss Dashwoods spent each entire day in Conduit Street. For their own comfort they would much rather have stayed at Mrs. Jennings's house, at least through the morning. But that preference could not be urged against everyone's wishes. Their hours were therefore handed over to Lady Middleton and the Miss Steeles, who in reality valued their company as little as they professed to desire it.

changes.before: In these moments of precious, priceless misery, she welcomed Cleveland with tears of anguish. Returning by another route, she felt all the happy privilege of freedom in the country, of wandering wherever she chose in unrestrained, luxurious solitude. She resolved to spend nearly every hour of every day with the Palmers indulging in these solitary walks.
changes.after: In these moments of precious, priceless misery, she rejoiced through tears of anguish that she was at Cleveland. Returning to the house by another route, she felt all the happy privilege of freedom in the country, of wandering wherever she chose in unrestrained, luxurious solitude. She resolved to spend nearly every hour of every day during her stay with the Palmers indulging in these solitary walks.

changes.before: Elinor had seen little of Mr. Palmer, and his behaviour towards her and Marianne had varied so much in that little, that she did not know what to expect of him at home. She found him entirely a gentleman towards his guests, and rude to his wife and her mother only occasionally. He could be a pleasant companion, and was kept from always being one chiefly by his readiness to imagine himself as superior to people generally as he must feel towards Charlotte and Mrs. Jennings. In the rest of his character and habits, Elinor noticed nothing unusual for a man of his age. He was particular about food, irregular in his hours, and fond of his child though he pretended to dismiss him. He wasted at billiards the mornings that ought to have been given to business. On the whole, however, she liked him much better than she had expected. Inwardly, she was not sorry she could like him no more: not sorry that his love of luxury, selfishness, and conceit made her turn with satisfaction to the thought of Edward's generosity, simple tastes, and modest feelings.

changes.before: Fearing that Marianne was tired, Elinor led her home. Until they reached the cottage door, she spoke only of Willoughby and their conversation. She could easily guess Marianne's curiosity, though no question expressed it, and supplied careful details of every word and look where such detail could safely be given. Once inside, Marianne kissed her gratefully. Through her tears she could just make out two words, “Tell Mama,” before leaving her sister and going slowly upstairs. Elinor would not disturb so reasonable a wish for solitude. Anxiously imagining its effect, and resolved to reopen the subject herself if Marianne did not, she entered the sitting room to carry out her sister's request.
